notes.en: The accounts agree that Hamas-led armed groups attacked Israel on 7 October 2023 and took hostages and that a war in Gaza followed; they differ on its legal characterisation (self-defence or genocide), on responsibility and on names (Hamas calls the attack Operation Al-Aqsa Flood). As of 18 October 2026 the ICJ had not ruled on the merits of South Africa v Israel; provisional measures are not findings that genocide occurred. Casualty figures are deliberately omitted; only counting methods are described.

title.en: Who controls the Temple Mount / al-Haram al-Sharif, what is its status quo, and what should it be called?

summary.en: The Israeli government calls the site the Temple Mount and treats it, with the Western Wall, as among the Jewish people's most holy sites, describing denial of that connection as a denial of history [1]. It states that it upholds the status quo under which Muslims pray on the Temple Mount and non-Muslims visit it, and that it has no intention of dividing the site [2]. Israel's Basic Law on Jerusalem commits the state to protect the holy places from desecration and to safeguard the freedom of access of members of all religions [3]. The arrangement dates from 1967, when Defence Minister Moshe Dayan left the Islamic Waqf in charge of the site and Israel in effect barred Jewish worship there to keep the peace [4].

sources.locator: statement of 13 Oct 2016, as reproduced by Daily Alert
sources.quote: To say that Israel has no connection to the Temple Mount is like saying that China has no connection to the Great Wall of China or that Egypt has no connection to the pyramids

sources.locator: statement of 24 Oct 2015, as quoted by JTA
sources.quote: Israel will continue to enforce its longstanding policy: Muslims pray on the Temple Mount; non-Muslims visit the Temple Mount

The Holy Places shall be protected from desecration and any other violation and from anything likely to violate the freedom of access of the members of the different religions to the places sacred to them
Defence Minister Moshe Dayan left the Waqf in control of the Esplanade, to avoid what he feared could be a major conflagration with the Arab and Islamic world.

label.en: Jewish religious opinion: rabbinic ban and Temple movements

summary.en: In the 1850s the rabbinic establishment in Palestine forbade Jews to ascend the site, lest they tread on the area of the ancient Temples' inner sanctum, and a sign placed by the rabbi of the Western Wall and the Holy Sites still says Jewish law prohibits entry [1]. Temple movement activists and some Israeli politicians argue that Jews should be free to pray at what they call Judaism's holiest site, and some activists hold that the old ruling was meant mainly to avoid clashes [1]. Analysts quoted by the International Crisis Group describe these activists as a small part of the national-religious public, though Temple activism rose after Israel's 2005 withdrawal from Gaza [1].

sources.quote: the rabbinic establishment in Palestine passed an interdiction on Jewish ascent, based on the Jewish legal principle that Jews were forbidden from treading on the inner sanctum of the ancient Temples

label.en: Palestinian position (PLO / State of Palestine and Muslim authorities)

summary.en: Palestinian leaders and Muslim religious authorities call the whole compound al-Masjid al-Aqsa or al-Haram al-Sharif, which a 2013 Jordan-PLO agreement defines as 144 dunums including the Qibli Mosque, the Dome of the Rock and all its mosques, buildings, walls and courtyards [1]. Many hold that the entire area, not only its buildings, is a mosque, and Muslim authorities such as the former mufti Ikrimah Sabri say Jews may enter as visitors but not as worshippers [2]. In this view Jewish prayer at the site would amount to a claim of ownership, which they reject [2]. The PLO holds that the compound lies within the territory of the State of Palestine, which has the right to sovereignty over all of it, including Jerusalem, while recognising the Jordanian king as custodian [1].

sources.locator: Preamble items C and G; Article 3.1
sources.quote: al-Masjid al-Aqsa with its 144 Dunums, which include the Qibli Mosque of al-Aqsa, the Mosque of the Dome of the Rock and all its mosques, buildings, walls, courtyards

summary.en: Under the 1994 Israel-Jordan peace treaty, Israel undertook to respect Jordan's present special role in the Muslim holy shrines of Jerusalem and to give high priority to that role in permanent status negotiations [1]. Jordan holds that the Hashemite kings have been custodians of Jerusalem's holy sites since 1924, a role the PLO and the Palestinian Authority recognised in a 2013 agreement with King Abdullah II [2]. Jordanian officials say they coordinate with Israel to keep public order at the site without recognising Israeli rights there [3].

sources.quote: Israel respects the present special role of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in Muslim Holy shrines in Jerusalem
The continuity of Hashemite King of Jordan’s custodianship of the Holy Sites since 1924

sources.locator: p. 5 fn. 15 (Jordanian diplomat, Crisis Group interview)
sources.quote: We coordinate de facto to keep public order. We do not recognise Israeli rights there.

summary.en: A 2016 draft decision on Occupied Palestine, submitted by seven Arab states and approved by UNESCO's Executive Board, referred to the site only as Al-Aqsa Mosque/Al-Haram Al-Sharif, called the Western Wall plaza Al-Buraq Plaza, and called on Israel, as occupying power, to restore the status quo that prevailed until September 2000, when the Jordanian Awqaf had exclusive authority [1][2]. The same text affirmed the importance of the Old City of Jerusalem and its walls for the three monotheistic religions [1]. UNESCO's head, Irina Bokova, responded that Jerusalem's heritage is indivisible and that denying or erasing any of its Jewish, Christian or Muslim traditions undermines the integrity of the site [3].

sources.quote: Affirming the importance of the Old City of Jerusalem and its Walls for the three monotheistic religions
Following UNESCO's adoption of a resolution which ignores the ties of the Jewish people to its most holy sites
To deny, conceal or erase any of the Jewish, Christian or Muslim traditions undermines the integrity of the site.

summary.en: The International Crisis Group uses the term Holy Esplanade to refer neutrally to what Jews call the Temple Mount and Muslims the Noble Sanctuary or al-Aqsa [1]. It describes the status quo as an informal modus vivendi that emerged after 1967, in which the Jordanian-run Waqf administers the site and non-Muslim prayer is barred, while Israel controls security [1][2]. It argues that the arrangement eroded after 2000, as Israel took sole control of non-Muslim entry and calls for Jewish prayer moved from marginal groups toward the political mainstream, developments that Palestinians and Jordan regard as a threat to the status quo [1].

sources.quote: The Holy Esplanade – the term this report uses to refer neutrally to what Jews call the Temple Mount and Muslims the Noble Sanctuary/Al-Aqsa
was the product of tacit pragmatism, not a formal understanding

notes.en: Names: Temple Mount (Hebrew Har haBayit) in Jewish and Israeli usage; al-Haram al-Sharif (the Noble Sanctuary) and al-Masjid al-Aqsa in Muslim and Palestinian usage, the latter increasingly for the whole compound; some neutral works use Holy Esplanade. All accounts agree the site is sacred to Muslims and Jews and that a status quo has governed worship since 1967; they disagree on sovereignty, on what the status quo requires (especially Jewish prayer and access) and on how far it has changed.
